title_en: Against the Cataphrygians, to Avircius Marcellus
author: Anonymous (anti-Montanist writer)
occasion: Avircius Marcellus commissioned a written refutation of the heresy associated with Miltiades. The author delayed out of caution, but after encountering the church at Ancyra in Galatia troubled by the new prophecy, he debated the Montanists there and now sends a written account.
argument: The author argues that the so-called new prophecy of Montanus and his female associates is a false prophecy, not the true prophetic gift promised by Christ. He shows that its origin was demonic, marked by ecstatic frenzy and love of preeminence, and that its prophets suffered no persecution and died shamefully. He refutes their appeal to martyrs and to prophetic succession, and insists that true prophecy never operates through ecstatic madness. The Montanist claim fails because no successors to Montanus and the women can be shown, though the prophetic gift should continue in the church until the final coming.

outline.move: The author explains his delay in writing, his recent debates at Ancyra, and his promise to send a written account.
He narrates the origin of the heresy: Montanus in Ardabau fell into ecstatic frenzy, two women were filled with the false spirit, and the Asian churches examined and rejected the movement.
He challenges the Montanists to name any of their prophets who were persecuted or killed for Christ, and reports the shameful deaths of Montanus, Maximilla, and Theodotus.

He cites Maximilla's saying and its refutation, notes that bishops Zoticus and Julian were silenced, and argues that Maximilla's prophecy of wars was false since peace has continued for over thirteen years.
He refutes the appeal to martyrs, showing that other heretics also have martyrs, and reports that church martyrs refused communion with Montanist martyrs.
He notes that he excerpted these arguments from a work opposing Miltiades' writing, which claimed a prophet should not speak in ecstasy.
He argues that false prophets speak in ecstatic madness, that no true prophet old or new did so, and that the Montanists cannot show successors to Montanus and the women.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Avircius Marcellus commissioned a written refutation of the heresy associated with Miltiades
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπιταχθεὶς ὑπὸ σοῦ συγγράψαι τινὰ λόγον εἰς τὴν τῶν κατὰ Μιλτιάδην λεγομένων αἵρεσιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Avircius Marcellus commissioned a written refutation of the heresy called 'that of those according to Miltiades' (τῶν κατὰ Μιλτιάδην λεγομένων αἵρεσιν), i.e., the heresy associated with Miltiades, not 'associated with Miltiades' as a target to be refuted. The phrasing is ambiguous: Miltiades may be the heretic or the opponent of the heresy.

_unresolved_facts.claim: he debated the Montanists there and now sends a written account
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: περὶ αὐτῶν τε τούτων καὶ τῶν προτεινομένων ὑπ' αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε διελέχθημεν ἡμέραις πλείοσιν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ... ἐπηγγειλάμεθα δὲ ἐνθάδε γράψαντες τοῦ Κυρίου διδόντος, διὰ σπουδῆς πέμψειν αὐτοῖς
_unresolved_facts.fix: he spoke in the church for several days about the Montanists and their claims, and promised to send a written account to the local elders (not 'now sends'—the text says he promised to send it)

_unresolved_facts.claim: He shows that its origin was demonic, marked by ecstatic frenzy and love of preeminence
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ ψυχῆς ἀμέτρῳ φιλοπρωτείας δόντα πάροδον εἰς ἑαυτὸν τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ, πνευματοφορηθῆναί τε καὶ αἰφνιδίως ἐν κατοχῇ τινὶ καὶ παρεκστάσει γενόμενον ἐνθουσιᾷν
_unresolved_facts.fix: He shows that its origin involved Montanus giving entry to 'the opposing one' (τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ, likely the devil) through immoderate desire for preeminence, and that he was spirit-carried and fell into ecstasy—'demonic' is an inference not explicit in the text

_unresolved_facts.claim: its prophets suffered no persecution and died shamefully
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἴσως μὲν γὰρ οὕτως, ἴσως δὲ οὐχ' οὕτως τετελευτήκασι Μοντανός τε καὶ Θεόδοτος καὶ ἡ προειρημένη γυνή
_unresolved_facts.fix: the author reports that they are said to have died shamefully but explicitly expresses uncertainty: 'perhaps thus, perhaps not thus did Montanus and Theodotus and the aforesaid woman die'

_unresolved_facts.claim: He challenges the Montanists to name any of their prophets who were persecuted or killed for Christ
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀποκρινάσθωσαν ἡμῖν πρὸς Θεοῦ ἔστι τὶς... ὅς τις ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων ἐδιώχθη, ἢ ὑπὸ παρανόμων ἀπεκτάνθη;
_unresolved_facts.fix: He challenges them to answer whether any of those who began speaking from Montanus and the women was persecuted by Jews or killed by lawless men—not specifically 'for Christ'

_unresolved_facts.claim: He cites Maximilla's saying and its refutation
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ μὴ λεγέτω ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ τῷ κατὰ Ἀστέριον Οὐρβανὸν τὸ διὰ Μαξιμίλλης πνεῦμα...
_unresolved_facts.fix: He cites what the spirit through Maximilla said, in a work against Asterius Urbanus, and challenges that spirit to demonstrate its power—the 'refutation' is his challenge, not a separate refutation

_unresolved_facts.claim: notes that bishops Zoticus and Julian were silenced
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὧν οἱ περὶ Θεμίσωνα τὰ στόματα φιμώσαντες, οὐκ εἴασαν τὸ ψευδὲς καὶ λαοπλάνον πνεῦμα ὑπ' αὐτῶν ἐλεγχθῆναι
_unresolved_facts.fix: notes that the followers of Themison silenced Zoticus and Julian, preventing the false spirit from being refuted by them

_unresolved_facts.claim: He notes that he excerpted these arguments from a work opposing Miltiades' writing
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ταῦτα... εὑρὼν ἔν τινι συγγράμματι αὐτῶν ἐνισταμένων τῷ Μιλτιάδου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ συγγράμματι
_unresolved_facts.fix: He notes that he excerpted these arguments from a work of the Montanists (αὐτῶν) opposing the writing of Miltiades the brother—'their work opposing Miltiades' brother's writing'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Miltiades: A writer whose work argued that a prophet should not speak in ecstasy; the Montanists opposed his writing
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τῷ Μιλτιάδου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ συγγράμματι, ἐν ᾧ ἀποδείκνυσι περὶ τοῦ μὴ δεῖν προφήτην ἐν ἐκστάσει λαλεῖν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Miltiades the brother (τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ): a writer whose work argued that a prophet should not speak in ecstasy; the Montanists opposed his writing. The brief omits 'the brother' which may indicate a specific known figure (possibly Miltiades of Athens)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Asterius Urbanus: Likely a Montanist defender; the saying of Maximilla is quoted from a work directed against him
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ τῷ κατὰ Ἀστέριον Οὐρβανὸν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Asterius Urbanus: The saying is quoted from a work 'against' him (κατὰ); he is likely a Montanist figure, but 'defender' is speculative—he could be the author of the work being cited or its target

_unresolved_facts.claim: Asterius Urbanus (quoted): The author summarizes and then quotes from a work against Asterius Urbanus; the 'he' in the summary refers to the author of that work
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ μὴ λεγέτω ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ τῷ κατὰ Ἀστέριον Οὐρβανὸν τὸ διὰ Μαξιμίλλης πνεῦμα...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The spirit through Maximilla is quoted; there is no indication that Asterius Urbanus is a speaker or quoted. The work is 'against Asterius Urbanus' or 'by Asterius Urbanus'—the syntax is ambiguous (τῷ κατὰ Ἀστέριον Οὐρβανὸν could mean 'the work by Asterius Urbanus' or 'the work against him')

_unresolved_facts.claim: Theodotus: An early leader of the Montanist prophecy, said to have died badly after being deceived
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸν θαυμαστὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν πρῶτον τῆς κατ' αὐτοὺς λεγομένης προφητείας οἷον ἐπίτροπον τινὰ Θεόδοτον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Theodotus: Called 'that wonderful one, the first of their so-called prophecy, like a trustee/curator (ἐπίτροπον)'; the brief's 'early leader' understates the sarcastic 'wonderful' (θαυμαστὸν, likely ironic)
